info.bio:
Malcolm Robert Andrew Edwards (Londres, Inglaterra, 22 de enero de 1946 - 7 de abril de 2010), mejor conocido como Malcolm McLaren, es un músico y empresario, mánager y productor británico que saltó a la fama como agente del famoso grupo de la primera ola del punk Sex Pistols.

Le atrajo el movimiento de la Internacional Situacionista, que promovía actos absurdos y de provocación, como medio de la promulgación de los cambios sociales. En 1968

scenes.name: Downtown: graffiti, punk y hip hop en el Mudd Club, Negril y el Roxy
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Fab 5 Freddy (Fred Brathwaite), del grupo de grafiteros de Brooklyn Fabulous 5 con Lee Quiñones, ofrecía en The Village Voice murales por encargo; con Michael Holman montó la Canal Zone Party (1979), donde apareció Jean-Michel Basquiat, mitad de SAMO, y llevó a Bambaataa al Mudd Club. La Zulu Nation y los Funky 4 + 1, que mezclaban punk y hip hop ante los Beastie Boys, bajaron al Ritz, el Mudd Club, Danceteria, Negril y el Roxy de Kool Lady Blue: en Negril, cedido por el mánager de los Clash, se juntaron por primera vez los cuatro elementos; en el Roxy, una pista de patinaje de la calle 18, Bambaataa, Afrika Islam y Grand Mixer D.ST pinchaban para Bianca Jagger, Warhol, la Rock Steady Crew o Madonna. Debbie Harry y Chris Stein (Blondie), amigos de Flash, nombraron a Freddy y a Flash en «Rapture» (1981), primer rap número 1 en Billboard, y llevaron a los Funky 4 + 1 a Saturday Night Live (14 de febrero de 1981), primera actuación de hip hop en la televisión nacional. Para Holman, sin el abrazo del downtown el hip hop no habría sido lo que fue; para Dante Ross, los negros se llevaron pantalones pitillo y opiáceos y los blancos toda esa cultura.
scenes.family: Cultura hip hop: graffiti, baile, cine, moda, política

scenes.name: Marley Marl y la Juice Crew
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Los noctámbulos del Disco Fever se bautizaron Juice Crew y Mr. Magic pasó a ser Sir Juice: el primer colectivo de estrellas, con la producción de Marley Marl. Becario de estudio en Queensbridge, Marley descubrió hacia 1985 que podía aislar el golpe de caja de un disco y tocar sus propios ritmos con un sampler: cambió el sonido del hip hop y, sampleando a James Brown («el primer b-boy»), abrió el camino a Pete Rock, DJ Premier, Large Professor o RZA. Cuando U.T.F.O. dejó plantado a Mr. Magic, Marley grabó con Lolita Gooden, de catorce años, «Roxanne’s Revenge», un ataque que desató docenas de respuestas y lanzó a Roxanne Shanté; siguieron MC Shan («Marley Marl Scratch», el inicio del boom bap), Craig G, Biz Markie, Big Daddy Kane, Kool G Rap y Masta Ace, casi todos en Cold Chillin’ (Fly Ty Williams y Len Fichtelberg), un sello que «robaba a sus artistas». «The Symphony» (1988), improvisada tras una sesión de fotos, con Ace, Craig G, G Rap (que rapeó hasta que se acabó la cinta) y Kane, fue uno de los primeros posse cuts. Queensbridge, el mayor complejo de vivienda pública del país, a un puente de Manhattan, dio también a Cormega, Havoc, Capone o Nas: «un gumbo de magnificencia», una Roma.
scenes.family: Nueva York: Def Jam, Queens y la edad de oro

scenes.name: Malcolm McLaren y Bow Wow Wow
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Tras perder a los Sex Pistols, McLaren se exilia en París, descubre la música africana y, con la moda pirata del siglo XVIII de Vivienne Westwood, concibe su contraataque al postpunk «para universitarios»: ritmos burundeses (Simon Jeffes enseña polirritmia a Adam and the Ants, a quienes luego roba la banda), glamour, sexualidad adolescente y piratería en cassette. Con la anglobirmana Annabella Lwin, de catorce años, nace Bow Wow Wow: «C·30 C·60 C·90 Go!» (1980), Your Cassette Pet, solo en cassette con caja de cigarrillos, «W.O.R.K.» (el paro como liberación: «conviértanse en piratas»). Anticipa el walkman, la world music y la música como banda sonora portátil, pero también manipula y explota a sus músicos (la revista nunca editada Chicken, fotos con menores). See Jungle! (1982) es una obra maestra del pop justo cuando él pierde el interés; «I Want Candy» triunfa en Estados Unidos. Boy George pasa brevemente por el grupo antes de fundar Culture Club.

scenes.name: Hip hop y la llegada del sampler
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Los DJ del Bronx aíslan y extienden los «breaks» de la música funk y disco: para McLaren, que hace un safari por el Bronx guiado por Michael Holman en 1981, el hip hop es «punk negro» y folklore urbano, piratería cultural pura. «Buffalo Gals» (1982), con el World's Famous Supreme Team, lleva el scratch al pop mainstream y siembra el jungle y el trip hop; Duck Rock mezcla Soweto, los Apalaches y el Bronx. Art of Noise inventa sin querer los breakbeats sampleados con el Fairlight antes que Marley Marl; ESG, Liquid Liquid y Art of Noise acaban entre los más sampleados del rap.

podcast.title: Encounter with Johnny Rotten (1975)
podcast.body: In 1975, Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop served as a significant location in music history. It was here that he encountered Johnny Rotten, who was wearing an "I Hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt, leading to Rotten's consideration for the lead singer role in the Sex Pistols. "Johnny Rotten walked into Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop in 1975. He was immediately considered for the job of lead singer of the sex pistols, based on the fact that he was wearing an eye-hate pink Floyd t-shirt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Punk Fashion Inspiration (1975)
podcast.body: During a 1975 trip to New York for a fashion fair, Malcolm McLaren took a detour to CBGBs, where he encountered Richard Hell, then bassist for The Heartbreakers. Hell, due to his poverty, wore ripped clothes held together with safety pins, a look McLaren misinterpreted as a "grand fashion statement," inspiring him to integrate safety pins into his own clothing designs back in England. "What drew Malcolm to Richard was a sense of style or what Malcolm thought to be Richard's sense of style because, well, you see, Richard was actually so poor that he'd wears clothing until they literally fell apart."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5

podcast.title: Final Illness and Legacy (2009-2010)
podcast.body: In October 2009, Malcolm McLaren was diagnosed with mesothelioma, a form of lung cancer often linked to asbestos exposure. He died on April 8, 2010, at a hospital in Switzerland. His burial featured a coffin spray-painted with "Too Fast to Live, Too Young to Die," and Sid Vicious's version of "My Way" was played. His headstone encapsulates his philosophy with the epitaph: "Better a Spectacular Failure than a benign success."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Adopting Hell's Aesthetic for Punk
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren, having previously managed the New York Dolls, was profoundly influenced by Richard Hell's visual style during his visit to New York. After Hell refused his offer to move to the UK, McLaren returned to London. There, he opened a clothing store named "Sex," directly inspired by Hell's distinctive manner of dressing, which he then used as the foundation for the Sex Pistols' image. "De vuelta a Londres, McLaren abrió una tienda de ropa inspirada en la forma de vestir de Hell, a la que llamó Sex."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)

podcast.title: Advocacy for Sid Vicious after Nancy's Death
podcast.body: After Nancy Spungin's murder and Sid Vicious's arrest, Malcolm McLaren and Sid's mother immediately sought a high-profile lawyer for his defense. McLaren strongly believed Sid was innocent, theorizing that an unknown guest had robbed the couple and then stabbed Nancy, noting that $20,000 in royalty money was missing from their room. "McLaren thought that Sid was innocent. He had a theory. He thought that the couple was robbed by an unknown guest who then stabbed Nancy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: British Airways Commercial Collaboration (1980s)
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren worked on TV advertisements for British Airways, famously arranging a piece called "The Flower Duet" with Greek composer Yanni. This piece was cribbed from the French opera *Lakmé* and became widely recognized as part of the "world's favorite airline" campaign.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Vivienne Westwood
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren co-owned a clothing store in Chelsea, London, with his partner Vivienne Westwood. Initially named "Let It Rock," the store specialized in Teddyboy fashion, bondage gear, and sex toys. Following McLaren's inspiration from Richard Hell, the store was later renamed "Sex" and began selling creations that incorporated safety pins, which became an iconic element of early punk fashion. "Before Malcolm McLaren hooked up with the pistols, he and his partner Vivian Westwood owned a clothing store in the Chelsea area of London called Let It Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5

podcast.title: Discovery of Richard Hell's Aesthetic
podcast.body: During his time in New York, Malcolm McLaren visited CBGB and saw Television perform. He was particularly struck by Richard Hell's aesthetic, recognizing its potential beyond just music, seeing Hell as a potential youth leader for a new movement. "Bansi BGB y B a los televisión, pero sobre todo le llama la atención la estética de Richard Hill."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Early Life and Fashion Career
podcast.body: Born in Yemen and raised by his grandmother in London, Malcolm McLaren attended various art schools before deciding on a career in fashion. He was always a schemer and, along with his girlfriend Vivienne Westwood, opened a shop at 430 Kings Road in London, initially called Paradise Garage in 1971. The shop evolved through names like Too Fast to Live, Too Young to Die and Sex, becoming a hub for unusual clothing, including fetish and bondage gear.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Embracing Hip Hop and Electronic Music (1980s)
podcast.body: In the early 1980s, Malcolm McLaren discovered rap and hip hop from New York and became a major evangelist for the new sound, incorporating these elements into his own records. He later ventured into electronic and club music, releasing a series of singles and albums that achieved success on the dance charts.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: False Claim to Authorship
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren claimed to be the "true architect" of the punk aesthetic. However, it was later revealed that he had copied the ideas, primarily from Richard Hell, making his claim false. "Mal con Maclaren reclamó ser el verdadero artífice de la estética punk y el resultado que era mentira."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Film, TV, and Art Ventures (1980s-1990s)
podcast.body: McLaren diversified his career into film and TV projects, serving as both a director and producer, and occasionally as a performer. He was also a painter and, in 1985, he took a job with CBS Films where he oversaw various productions, including a movie titled "Heavy Metal Serving Nazis." He was also involved in a biopic about Led Zeppelin manager Peter Grant.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation of Sex Pistols
podcast.body: Following his return to London and the opening of his "Sex" store, Malcolm McLaren gathered a group of misfits. He provided them with clothes, instruments, and a name—the Sex Pistols—effectively engineering the creation of one of punk's most iconic bands. "Poco después juntó una panda de inalaptados. Los vistió, les dio un instrumento a cada uno y les puso un nombre. Sex pistols."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)

podcast.title: Importer of Punk Aesthetic to London
podcast.body: After failing to bring Richard Hell to London for a solo career, Malcolm McLaren returned to the United Kingdom, carrying with him the aesthetic ideas he had observed from Richard Hell in New York. This was a pivotal moment in transferring the punk look across the Atlantic. "Malcomma claren vuelve al reino unido con la idea estética que había tenido de Richard Hill y ahí es cuando la exporta a su esposa que es la gran diseñadora Vivian Westwood."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: New York Dolls Management
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren, owner of a "small, weird clothing shop in London," ventured into band management after encountering the New York Dolls during a clothing show in New York. When the Dolls were dropped from their record deal and sought new management, McLaren, despite his inexperience, stepped in with ambitious plans. He envisioned a radical image makeover for the band, proposing red leather attire instead of their previous spandex and makeup, and using a large Soviet flag as a live backdrop, a move that proved to be less appealing to their original fanbase. "His name was Malcolm McLaren, and he chanced upon the dolls when he was in New York for a clothing show."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New York Dolls Manager
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren served as one of the early managers for the New York Dolls. His time in New York placed him in a position to observe the emerging punk aesthetic. "Malcomma claren era el manager fracasador de los New Yorkers. El año y oro subieron como varios managers y uno de los primeros managers que tuvieron en el malcomma claren que era británico."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: New York Dolls and Band Management
podcast.body: After a trip to a New York fashion fair in 1973, Malcolm McLaren became deeply interested in the New York Dolls and decided to try his hand at band management. This initial venture was a disaster, and the Dolls soon broke up, but McLaren remained undeterred.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Owner of "Sex" Clothing Shop
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren owned the clothing shop named "Sex" on Kings Road in Chelsea, London. This shop served as a hub for the early punk scene and was where he recruited John Lighten for the Sex Pistols. "All four hung around a clothing shop called Sex on the Kings Road in Chelsea, which is where owner Malcolm McLaren recruited John Lighten to be the singer of a group."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Payment Strategy for Sid Vicious
podcast.body: During the Sex Pistols' chaotic US tour, McLaren put Sid Vicious on a weekly stipend of $14, hoping that a lack of readily available cash might help him "keep him straight" from drug use. "McLaren had him on a weekly stipend of $14, thinking that maybe a lock of cash would keep him straight."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Political Ambition and Reality TV (1990s-2000s)
podcast.body: In 1999, Malcolm McLaren launched a campaign to be mayor of London, famously promising to allow public libraries to serve alcohol, though he never made it to Election Day. In the 2000s, he became a regular on reality TV shows like *Big Brother*.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Dolls Plans
podcast.body: After the New York Dolls ultimately fell apart following a couple of tours under his management, Malcolm McLaren returned to England. He carried with him "definite ideas on what he'd do next time," suggesting his experience with the Dolls significantly shaped his future endeavors in the music industry. "But all was not lost. Because Malcolm McLaren went back to his shop in England with some definite ideas on what he'd do next time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reaction to Sid Vicious's Violence
podcast.body: After Sid Vicious assaulted journalist Nick Kent with a bicycle chain in June 1976, McLaren expressed dismay, calling Sid a "psychopath" and promising that he would never be allowed at their concerts again. "Malcolm McLaren though was mortified. He told Kent, oh God, that guy's a psychopath. He'll never be one of our concerts again. I promise that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Sex Pistols Manager and Stylist
podcast.body: As the manager of the Sex Pistols, Malcolm McLaren decided that the band should adopt and wear the clothes being sold and designed by his wife, Vivienne Westwood, at their shop, making them key figures in popularizing the aesthetic. "Malcomma claren sería el manadier que haría famos usados a los 6 pistos y sería el que tomaría la idea de que los 6 pistos deberían llevar un poco la ropa y las ideas que se estaba vendiendo y que estaba haciendo Vivian Westwood."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Strategy for Sex Pistols US Tour
podcast.body: For the Sex Pistols' 1977 US tour, McLaren conceived a "subversive" strategy to tour the punk-unfriendly Southern US, believing it would be "very punk." "McLaren thought it would be very subversive, very punk, if the pistols made a big swing into the punk, unfriendly, southern US."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Vision for Sex Pistols
podcast.body: McLaren recruited John Lighten to be the singer of a group that would serve as a "living breathing advertisement" for his clothing store, "Sex," which he then named the Sex Pistols. "Malcolm McLaren recruited John Lighten to be the singer of a group that would be a living breathing advertisement for his store. He called them the Sex Pistols."

xref.title: Formation Anecdote (1975)
xref.body: The formation of the Sex Pistols and Johnny Rotten's recruitment in 1975 is marked by a notable anecdote involving Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop. Rotten's "I Hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt served as an instant identifier of his anti-establishment attitude, leading to his consideration as the band's frontman. "He was immediately considered for the job of lead singer of the sex pistols, based on the fact that he was wearing an eye-hate pink Floyd t-shirt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Johnny Rotten's Audition (1975)
xref.body: In 1975, Malcolm McLaren, the former manager of The New York Dolls and co-proprietor of the "Sex" clothing shop at 430 King's Road in London's Chelsea area, sought to form a band as a living advertisement for his store. He liked the name "Pistols" for its dangerous connotation, thus "Sex Pistols." Malcolm was looking for a singer and was introduced to 19-year-old Johnny Lydon (later Johnny Rotten), who had green teeth and was spotted by Bernie Rhodes wearing a homemade "I hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt held together with safety pins. Despite Lydon's inability to sing, Malcolm had him audition by miming and "singing" Alice Cooper's "I'm 18" to a jukebox in the shop, which landed him the role. "So Malcolm got young John to audition, not caring if Johnny could actually sing a note, which he couldn't."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

xref.title: Formation and Vision (1975)
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren conceived the Sex Pistols as a living, breathing advertisement for his Kings Road shop, which by then was renamed Sex. The band was also intended to be an outlet for McLaren's semi-seditious political beliefs, designed to shock and shake up the stuffy British establishment. McLaren assembled the group using "snotty kids" who frequented his store, naming them "Sex" after his shop and "Pistols" because it sounded dangerous.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sex Pistols Audition (1975)
xref.body: In 1975, Johnny Rotten was considered for the lead singer position of the Sex Pistols after walking into Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop. His distinctive appearance, specifically wearing an "I Hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt, immediately caught attention and played a role in his consideration for the band. "Johnny Rotten walked into Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop in 1975. He was immediately considered for the job of lead singer of the sex pistols, based on the fact that he was wearing an eye-hate pink Floyd t-shirt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

xref.title: Unwitting Punk Fashion Catalyst (1975)
xref.body: In 1975, while serving as the bassist for The Heartbreakers, Richard Hell met Malcolm McLaren at CBGBs in New York. Due to his impoverished circumstances, Hell wore his clothing until it literally fell apart, then used safety pins to hold the ripped scraps together. McLaren, misinterpreting this as a deliberate "grand fashion statement," adopted the idea and brought it back to England, where it became a cornerstone of nascent punk fashion. "What drew Malcolm to Richard was a sense of style or what Malcolm thought to be Richard's sense of style because, well, you see, Richard was actually so poor that he'd wears clothing until they literally fell apart. And once they did that, he'd hold the rip scraps of cloth together with safety pins."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5

xref.title: Bill Grundy Show Appearance (December 1, 1976)
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren, the band's manager, was contacted by Bill Grundy's office for a last-minute appearance on the "Today" show after Queen cancelled. The band and their entourage, already heavily inebriated from bottles of wine consumed in the limo, were escorted onto the live TV set at 6:15pm. During the interview, members of the band engaged in swearing on air, leading to Bill Grundy's TV career ending by 6:18pm and the country being shocked. "Someone in Bill Grundy's office got a hold of Malcolm McLaren, the manager of a new group called the Sex Pistols, who had just released their debut single a week earlier."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Malcolm McLaren's Use of "New Wave" (1976)
xref.body: In late 1976, Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren, described as a "very artsy guy," was quoted in *Melody Maker* magazine using the term "new wave." He applied it to bands that, while related to punk and sharing its core "seam," did not necessarily embody a strictly "punk" sound, thus helping to popularize the term. "Later that year, late 76, a story in Melody Maker magazine quoted Sex Pistols Manager Malcolm McLaren, very artsy guy. And he was using the term and applying it to bands that were related to punk, part of the same seamst punk, but not necessarily sounding that punk at all."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Record Label Controversies (1976-1977)
xref.body: The Sex Pistols, managed by Malcolm McLaren's Glitter Best, first secured a deal with EMI Records. However, they were soon dropped due to their controversial nature and were essentially paid to leave. Next, they signed with A&M Records, a contract that notoriously lasted only five days before the band was again paid to go away. Their third and final deal was with Virgin Records, and this one "stuck," allowing the Sex Pistols to become a sensation and indeed challenge the British establishment.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: A&M Records Contract Termination and Payout (March 16, 1977)
xref.body: Six days after signing with A&M Records and trashing their London offices, the Sex Pistols were dropped by the label on March 16, 1977, partly due to objections from other A&M acts like Captain & Tennille. Manager Malcolm McLaren was informed the decision was for "humane reasons." Although the band did not receive the full 150,000 pounds from their contract, they were paid 75,000 pounds, a significant sum for less than a week's work. "The pistols didn't collect their 150,000 pounds, but they did walk away with 75,000 pounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 6

xref.title: Glenn Matlock's Departure (February 1977)
xref.body: Matlock's departure was officially reported as a firing in February 1977 because he "liked The Beatles too much," specifically Paul McCartney, and allegedly washed his feet too often. This narrative was fabricated and fed to the press by manager Malcolm McLaren. In truth, Matlock quit due to intense friction with Johnny Rotten, McLaren's manipulative "head games," constant media attacks, canceled gigs, venue bans, lack of pay, and the physical assaults suffered by Johnny and Paul. "Glenn Matlock was fired in February 1977... Matlock wasn't fired. He quit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joining Sex Pistols as Bassist – February 1977
xref.body: After Glenn Matlock was fired from the Sex Pistols in February 1977, manager Malcolm McLaren decided to replace him with a fan. Sid was chosen because he was always around and was Johnny Rotten's friend, embodying the punk ethos of the ultimate fan joining the ultimate band. "Malcolm McLaren came up with the idea of hiring one of the group's fans as his replacement."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious' Recruitment (1977)
xref.body: In the spring of 1977, Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren insisted on Sid Vicious joining the band as a replacement for original bassist Glenn Matlock, who was allegedly fired for liking The Beatles too much. McLaren's decision was not based on Vicious's musical ability—he "couldn't name the strings on a bass, let alone play them"—but on the idea that it would be "cool if a fan was invited to join the group."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

xref.title: Come on Everybody (1978) – Eddie Cochran Cover

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Disastrous American Tour and Final Performance (1978)
xref.body: The Sex Pistols' American tour culminated in their final performance at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco on January 14, 1978. The tour was marred by hostile audiences, Sid Vicious's extreme intoxication and altercations, Malcolm McLaren's difficult management, and deep internal animosity, all of which were captured in the film "The Great Rock and Roll Swindle." This show marked the last time the original lineup would perform together for nearly 18 years, and the final appearance with Sid Vicious before his death 13 months later. "It shows a band at the end of their rope and literally ready to blow apart."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5

xref.title: Disastrous American Tour – Deep South, 1978
xref.body: Manager Malcolm McLaren planned for the Sex Pistols' first American tour to go through the "deep conservative South" in an attempt to be subversive. The tour proved to be a disaster, marked by Sid Vicious's uncontrollable behavior and the band's self-destruction. "Manager Malcolm McLaren thought it would be really subversive if the pistols first tour of America was through the deep self."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Disastrous American Tour – January 1978
xref.body: Manager Malcolm McLaren's plan to "conquer America" with the Sex Pistols resulted in one of rock history's most disastrous road trips. Initially, the group's visa applications were denied, forcing them to cancel an important appearance on Saturday Night Live, where Elvis Costello was called in as a last-minute replacement. The drummer for Elvis Costello's performance notably wore a t-shirt that read "Thanks, milk," a sarcastic jab at Malcolm McLaren. McLaren made a bizarre miscalculation about American culture by routing the tour away from major cities and through the deep South, an area not receptive to punk rock values. "Instead, what he got was one of the most disastrous road trips in the history of rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Disputes with Manager Malcolm McLaren (1978)
xref.body: As the Sex Pistols gained fame, members, particularly singer Johnny Rotten, grew suspicious of Malcolm McLaren, accusing him of mismanagement of "everything, really." The band frequently found that there was no money available when they wanted to get paid. This deteriorating relationship culminated in the band's implosion at the end of a disastrous American tour in 1978.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Litigation and Control (1978-1987)
xref.body: Following the Sex Pistols' implosion in 1978, years of litigation ensued involving the band members and Malcolm McLaren's management company, Glitter Best. It took until 1987, nearly a decade after their breakup, for the Sex Pistols to finally wrestle away control of their music from McLaren.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Malcolm McLaren Posts Bail – October 17, 1978
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren posted Sid's $50,000 bail, leading to his release from Rikers Island on October 17, 1978. "October 17, 1978. Malcolm McLaren posts Sid's bail and he's released."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Move to New York City – August 1978
xref.body: With nowhere to go after their eviction, Sid and Nancy decided to move to New York City in August 1978, a place where Nancy claimed to know people. This move was partly funded by a £10,000 loan from Malcolm McLaren. "With nowhere to go, they decided that it was time to move to New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Advertising Vehicle for "Sex" Shop
xref.body: The Sex Pistols were originally conceived and formed with the primary purpose of serving as a living, breathing advertisement for the clothing shop named "Sex," which was run by their manager, Malcolm McLaren. The band was designed as nothing more than a promotional vehicle for the store's avant-garde and punk fashion. "the sex pistols were originally formed as a band that would primarily be a living, breathing advertisement for the clothing shop run by their manager, Malcolm McLaren. The shop was called Sex. And the sex pistols were originally designed as nothing more than an advertising vehicle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Annabella Lewin Nude Photoshoot
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren convinced Annabella Lewin, the group's underage lead singer, to pose nude in a sex magazine called *Chicken*, which McLaren himself had created. This incident added to McLaren's controversial management practices.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Attempted Marriage to Sid Vicious for Work Permit
xref.body: While working illegally in the UK, Chrissie Hynde, then employed at Malcolm McLaren's "Sex" shop, paid Sid Vicious two pounds to marry her so she could obtain a work permit. The plan was thwarted when the office where they intended to marry was closed on the chosen day. "She paid Sid two pounds to marry her so she could get a work permit. And it almost happened too, but the day they went to get married, the office was closed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

xref.title: Band Formation by Malcolm McLaren
xref.body: The Sex Pistols were conceived and formed by Malcolm McLaren, who co-owned the "Sex" shop at 430 King's Road with Vivienne Westwood. McLaren's intention was for the band to serve as a living, breathing advertisement for his store and Westwood's punk clothing designs after they transitioned from selling Teddyboy gear in 1975. "In 1975, Malcolm McLaren and Vivian Westwood had stopped selling clothes to teddy boys, and were now catering to punk kids. It was in this shop that Malcolm McLaren came up with the idea of forming a band that would be a living, breathing advertisement for his store and Vivian's clothing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Chrissie Hynde Association
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde of The Pretenders worked in Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop during the Sex Pistols' formative years. She also famously considered marrying Sid Vicious, the band's bassist, primarily to secure the British equivalent of a green card and remain in the UK. "Along with working in Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop in the earliest days of the Sex Pistols, she also wrote about punk in one of the British music magazines."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Chrissie Hynde's Punk Credentials
xref.body: Lead singer Chrissie Hynde, originally from Akron, Ohio, moved to the UK and became deeply involved in the early punk scene, working at Malcolm McLaren's shop "Sex" and playing guitar in bands that morphed into The Clash and The Damned, even considering a marriage of convenience with Sid Vicious. "So yeah, a lot of bonafide punk credentials."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

xref.title: Collaboration with Malcolm McLaren
xref.body: Vivienne Westwood co-owned a clothing store in Chelsea, London, with her partner Malcolm McLaren. The store, initially called "Let It Rock," focused on fashion for Teddyboys, bondage gear, and sex toys. After McLaren's pivotal trip to New York, the store was rebranded as "Sex" and became instrumental in popularizing punk fashion by selling garments held together with safety pins, a style inspired by Richard Hell. "Before Malcolm McLaren hooked up with the pistols, he and his partner Vivian Westwood owned a clothing store in the Chelsea area of London called Let It Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5

xref.title: Connection to Sex Pistols' Origins
xref.body: Inspired by Richard Hell's fashion, Malcolm McLaren used the safety pin aesthetic at his London store, Sex, and eventually conceived the idea of forming a band, the Sex Pistols, to act as a living advertisement for the shop. "McLaren then imported Richard's safety pin look back to Britain and opened a clothing shop that sold these kinds of clothes. The store became a magnet for young, disaffected kids. And to promote his store, Malcolm came up with the idea of forming a band that would be a living, breathing advertisement for the place. This store was called Sex. And the name of this band would be the Sex Pistols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest All-Time Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders: Part 1

xref.title: Demise of the Band
xref.body: After a couple of tours under Malcolm McLaren's management, the band began to fall apart. By March 1975, while on the road in Florida, the Dolls were nearing their end, as evidenced by surviving live recordings from that period. Shortly after this, the band was "done." "Short time later, they were done."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Designed to Showcase Fashion
xref.body: Bow Wow Wow was a group specifically designed by Malcolm McLaren for nothing more than to showcase Vivienne Westwood's new fashions. McLaren continued his trend of intertwining fashion and music with this project.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Filming for "The Great Rock and Roll Swindle" – Paris Trip
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren had the idea for Sid to continue as the new singer for the Sex Pistols. Sid traveled to Paris to film sequences for the movie "The Great Rock and Roll Swindle," performing Eddie Cochran songs. This trip was awful due to Sid and Malcolm's animosity and Nancy's continued drug supply. "The Sex Pistols could carry on with Sid as the new singer. So it was off to Paris in a cloud of junk to film a couple of sequences for a film that would end up being called the Great Rock and Roll Swindle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Naming
xref.body: The band's manager, Malcolm McLaren, assembled the group as a "living, breathing advertisement" for his store called Sex. The band's name, Sex Pistols, derived "Sex" from the store and "Pistols" because it sounded dangerous and "emish." "He called the band Sex Pistols, Sex after the store and pistols because, well, that sounded dangerous and weirdly as an emish."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Vision
xref.body: The Sex Pistols were formed when clothing shop owner Malcolm McLaren recruited John Lighten (who became Johnny Rotten) to be the singer for a group intended as a "living breathing advertisement" for his store, "Sex." "Malcolm McLaren recruited John Lighten to be the singer of a group that would be a living breathing advertisement for his store. He called them the Sex Pistols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

xref.title: Formation by Malcolm McLaren
xref.body: The Sex Pistols were formed when Malcolm McLaren "corralled" four kids who frequented his Sex boutique on King's Road, turning them into the band. Their formation and subsequent impact were pivotal for British punk rock. "Four of those kids were corralled by McLaren and he turned them into the sex pistols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 2

xref.title: Formation in Malcolm McLaren's Shop – King's Road
xref.body: The Sex Pistols were formed in Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop located on King's Road in London. This location served as a hub for the nascent punk scene. "The place where the Sex Pistols were formed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formed in a Clothing Shop
xref.body: The Sex Pistols were formed in a clothing shop owned and operated by Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood, who were designers specializing in fetish and bondage gear. The band's initial aesthetic was directly inspired by McLaren's observation of New York punk Richard Hell, who used safety pins to hold his decomposing clothes together, a look Vivienne Westwood subsequently introduced in their shop. "A few years later, the sex pistols were formed in a clothing shop run by a couple of designers of fetish and bondage gear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Funding for New York Move – Gig Money and McLaren Loan
xref.body: The money earned from the Electric Ballroom gig, combined with a £10,000 loan (in £10 notes) from Malcolm McLaren, funded Sid and Nancy's flight to New York City. "With the money from that gig at the Electric Ballroom in a 10,000-pound loan from Malcolm McLaren... Sid and Nancy flew to New York City."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Glenn Matlock's Departure
xref.body: Original bass player Glenn Matlock left the band before the release of "God Save the Queen." His departure was reportedly due to his perceived excessive affection for The Beatles. "Original bass player Glenn Matlock was out, apparently because he professed too much love for the Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ill-Fated Only American Tour
xref.body: The Sex Pistols embarked on their one and only tour of America with manager Malcolm McLaren's "insane idea" to play out-of-the-way, "redneck" markets in the Deep South instead of major cities, leading to predictable chaos and hostility. "This is exactly what happened with Sid Vicious during the Sex Pistols, one and only two-er of America. Manager Malcolm McLaren had this insane idea. Instead of playing all the big markets across the US, the group would duck down into the deep south and play out of the way markets that were decidedly not punk-friendly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Punk Fashion
xref.body: Richard Hell's distinctive safety-pin-adorned clothing caught the attention of UK band manager Malcolm McLaren in New York. McLaren subsequently brought this "safety pin look" to Britain, incorporating it into his clothing shop "Sex," which became a popular spot for disaffected youth. "So Richard wore his clothes until they fell apart. In fact, he wore them even after they fell apart, holding things together with safety pins. This went a wannabe band manager from the UK named Malcolm McLaren, saw Richard in New York and thought he had brilliant fashion sense."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest All-Time Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders: Part 1

xref.title: Kevin Mooney's Marriage to Jordan
xref.body: Kevin Mooney, a member of Adam and the Ants (another band managed by Malcolm McLaren), married Jordan Mooney after her time working at the Sex boutique. This connection highlights the intertwining relationships within the early British punk scene. "Jordan eventually married Kevin Mooney of Adam and the Ants, another one of Malcolm McLaren's bands and the job at sex ended."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 2

xref.title: King's Road Origins
xref.body: The Sex Pistols came together at Sex, Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop located on King's Road, a central location in the early punk scene. "She worked at Sex, Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop in the King's Road, where the sex pistols came together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

xref.title: Limited Income After Sex Pistols
xref.body: After the Sex Pistols disbanded in January 1978, Sid Vicious lacked a reliable income source. He did not contribute to writing any of the band's songs, meaning he received no significant royalty checks. Furthermore, the financial arrangements made by the band's manager, Malcolm McLaren, provided him with very little income. He relied on the generosity of friends and meager earnings from solo performances, with any money going towards rent, food, music gear, and heroin. "He was reduced to relying on the kindness of friends and to the meager amounts he received as a solo performer in the post sex pistols world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

xref.title: Malcolm McLaren's Association
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren, who was at one time their manager, started using the term "new wave" to describe cool new bands that weren't quite punk. "Malcolm McLaren, a one-time manager of the New York dolls, started throwing at the term when he was trying to describe cool new bands that weren't quite punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

xref.title: Malcolm McLaren's Management
xref.body: After being dropped from their record deal, the band hired Malcolm McLaren, the inexperienced but ambitious owner of a small, unusual clothing shop in London, as their new manager. McLaren, who discovered the Dolls during a New York clothing show, envisioned a complete image makeover, replacing their spandex, makeup, and big hair with red leather. He also proposed using a big Soviet flag as a stage backdrop for live performances, a move deemed not particularly smart at the time and less engaging than their previous sexual weirdness. "He thought the dolls needed a complete image makeover. That would fix everything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Malcolm McLaren's Management Practices
xref.body: The financial arrangements orchestrated by the band's manager, Malcolm McLaren, were such that Sid Vicious did not receive much income from his time with the Sex Pistols. "And with the way things were arranged through the pistols manager, Malcolm McLaren, there really wasn't much of an income stream for Sid."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

xref.title: Malcolm McLaren's Prior Management
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren, who later formed the Sex Pistols, was the failed manager of the New York band The New York Dolls prior to his venture with the Sex Pistols in 1975. "In 1975, Malcolm McLaren was the failed manager of a New York band called The New York Dolls."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

xref.title: Malcolm McLaren's Unmade Movie
xref.body: Manager Malcolm McLaren was plotting to create a movie featuring the Sex Pistols. He intended to use a softcore porn director for the project and hired an unknown screenwriter, Roger Ebert, who would later become a renowned film critic. "Meanwhile Malcolm McLaren was scheming to make a movie with the pistols using a soft core porn director and an unknown screenwriter named Roger Ebert."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Malcolm McLaren's Use of "New Wave"
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren, the manager of the Sex Pistols, frequently used the term "New Wave" in interviews. This contributed to Seymour Stein's consideration of the term for Sire Records' marketing campaign. "Malcolm McLaren, who was still the manager of the Sex Bistels at the time, peppered some of his interviews with this term."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

xref.title: Managed by Malcolm McLaren
xref.body: After his tumultuous tenure with the Sex Pistols, Malcolm McLaren went on to manage other acts, including Adam and the Ants. This was part of McLaren's continued involvement in the music industry following the punk rock era.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Managed by Malcolm McLaren
xref.body: Following his work with the full band, Adam, from Adam and the Ants, was later managed individually by Malcolm McLaren. McLaren continued to manage artists after the Sex Pistols.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Manager Malcolm McLaren
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren, the manager of the Sex Pistols, achieved a level of fame that was almost comparable to that of his band. "The special manager, Malcolm McLaren, was almost more famous than his band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Manager Malcolm McLaren's Manipulation
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren actively fostered animosity between Glenn Matlock and Johnny Rotten, setting them up to play "head games" with each other. He also created the false story of Matlock being fired for liking The Beatles, disseminating it to the press immediately after Matlock left. "Malcolm McLaren set it up so the two were always playing head games with each other."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Manager Malcolm McLaren's Recollection of Sid Vicious's Violence
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren recounted an incident from the American tour near San Antonio where Sid Vicious, heavily involved in drugs and eating knickerbocker glories, took offense to a family's rude comments about him at a restaurant. Sid then slashed the arm of the father with a pen knife, causing blood to spray onto his steak, terrifying onlookers. "He went round to the back of the gentleman that was eating his steak and chips and pulled his sleeve back and threw his arm over and above the man's head and over the man's plate up fairly high and withdrew a pen knife from his pocket and slashed his arm and all the blood blew out like ketchup over the man's steak."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: McLaren Management Proposal Rejected (Early 1980s)
xref.body: In the early 1980s, Malcolm McLaren approached the Red Hot Chili Peppers, a new band from LA, with the idea of managing them to incorporate hip hop and funk influences with a punk rock attitude. However, the band found McLaren untrustworthy and rejected his offer.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: McLaren's Attempted Re-hiring of Matlock
xref.body: Two weeks after Matlock's departure, Malcolm McLaren called him, acknowledging that his replacement, Sid Vicious, was not working out and asked Matlock to rejoin the band. Matlock refused, stating it was "too late" and he wanted "none of you locked anymore." "What if Madlock had returned to the Sex Pistols? How would their future and their legend and myth and legacy turned out?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pete Thomas's "Thanks, Malcolm" T-shirt on SNL
xref.body: During Elvis Costello's famous Saturday Night Live performance on December 17, 1977, drummer Pete Thomas wore a t-shirt emblazoned with "Thanks, Malcolm." This was a direct jab at Malcolm McLaren, the manager of the Sex Pistols, whose visa screw-up inadvertently opened the door for Costello's iconic appearance. "By the way, if you ever get to see that performance from December 17th, 1977, take a look at the t-shirt worn by drummer Pete Thomas. It says, thanks, Malcolm."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Elvis Costello

xref.title: Pioneering Safety Pin Fashion
xref.body: Richard Hell was so poor that his clothes were literally falling apart, and he held them together with safety pins. Malcolm McLaren was "particularly taken" with this look, considering it a "brilliant fashion statement" which he then brought back to England to sell at his store. "This guy was so poor that his clothes were literally falling apart and the only way he could wear anything was to hold his clothes together with safety pins."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Record Deal and Decline
xref.body: The "outrageous" New York Dolls had a record deal with a major label but were "well on their way to losing it." Malcolm McLaren briefly managed them in their "very last days." "The outrageous New York dolls had a record deal with a major label, although they were well on their way to losing it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Richard Hell's Safety Pins – Origin of Punk Fashion Adopted by McLaren and Westwood
xref.body: The punk fashion of wearing safety pins, later popularized worldwide by Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood, originated with Richard Hell of Television and the Voidoids in New York, who used them out of poverty to hold his torn clothing together. "The punk safety pin fashion was inspired by Richard Hell, who used them out of poverty to hold his clothes together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Role in Sex Pistols Formation – Led to McLaren's Shop
xref.body: Sid's interest in fashion was key to the Sex Pistols' origin. It was he who led his friends into Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop in King's Road, the very place where the Sex Pistols were formed. "Sid's fashion victimness is key to the Sex Pistols story because it was he who led everyone into Malcolm Clarence's clothing shop in the King's Road, the place where the Sex Pistols were formed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious Stabbing Incident
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren recounted an incident during the ill-fated American tour where Sid Vicious, deeply involved in drugs, became agitated in a motel restaurant near San Antonio. While sitting near a family eating, Vicious, wearing a dirty black t-shirt with a swastika and his feet black from not taking off his boots for six months, heard rude comments about him. He then walked behind the gentleman, pulled back his sleeve, threw his arm over the man's head and plate, and slashed his arm with a pen knife, causing blood to spurt out "like ketchup" over the man's steak. This occurred in a place full of "red necky guys" and "long distance truck drivers," leading McLaren to fear for their lives. "He went round to the back of the gentleman that was eating his steak and chips and pulled his sleeve back and threw his arm over and above the man's head and over the man's plate up fairly high and withdrew a pen knife from his pocket and slashed his arm and all the blood blew out like ketchup over the man's steak."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Subversive US Tour Strategy
xref.body: Instead of hitting major markets, manager Malcolm McLaren designed a "subversive" strategy for the US tour, planning a major swing into the punk-unfriendly Southern US. This tour, however, "did not go well," with hostile crowds and Sid Vicious often being too strung out to perform effectively. "But instead of hitting all the major markets, McLaren thought it would be very subversive, very punk, if the pistols made a big swing into the punk, unfriendly, southern US."
